zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: supplied [Entry Words Data of Nippojisho](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Consulted after independent scan reading; the transcription corrections and English notes are this reviewer's work, not a reproduction of the lexical dataset.

runs.text: Ley, ou cuſtume que corre por decen-

lines.note: Kehō denotes a family's inherited rule or custom. The final letter of Ley is y, not the OCR's x; the Portuguese word for descent begins here and continues below.

runs.text: dencia em algũa caſa, ou familia.

lines.note: Completes decendencia: the rule is transmitted within a house or family. The printed historical spelling is retained rather than modernized to descendência.
Kega is glossed as an error or mishap. The large initial is Q, not D; Qegano begins the expression for an unexpectedly fortunate result of a mishap.
Kega no kōmyō de gozaru describes an accidental achievement or lucky success. Mon. remains the printed citation label; the Portuguese explanation continues on the next row.

runs.text: feito do deſaſtre: vſaſe nas couſas que a cer-

lines.note: The gloss explains an achievement arising from a mishap, used of things that happen to turn out well. Preserve the printed separation a cer- and its physical continuation.

runs.text: tão de ſair bem, & milhoradas por algum ca-

lines.note: Completes acertão and specifies a good or improved outcome brought about by some chance event. Milhoradas is the printed historical vowel form; ca- continues as caso.
After completing caso, the entry gives kega wo suru or kaku, suffering a mishap. The spaced Portuguese A cõ- begins acontecer across the line break; l marks an alternative.

runs.text: tecer deſaſtre, ou couſa que redunda em dano,

lines.note: Completes acontecer and describes an event resulting in harm. The list of consequences continues below, so this is not an independent entry.
Shame completes the preceding list of harm caused by a mishap. This short continuation belongs to Qega and must remain a separate physical row.
Kegarawashii means unclean or defiling, directly matching immunda. The following two indented rows give related forms rather than new Portuguese definitions.
Kegarawashisa is the nominal form, uncleanness or impurity, derived from the preceding adjective. The long s belongs to the suffix and is not f.
Kegarawashū is the contracted adverbial form associated with kegarawashii. The final vowel visibly carries a caron; no missing gloss is supplied.
Kegare, kegaruru, kegareta gives the intransitive verb for becoming soiled. The example starts chi wo fukunde, with fu- continuing on the next physical row.

runs.text: cunde fitoni faqeba, mazzu ſono cuchi

lines.note: The example says that when one spits blood at another person, one's own mouth is affected first. Fukunde and hakeba are coherent verb forms; their printed spelling remains unchanged.

runs.text: O que tendo ſangue na boca coſpe

lines.note: Kegaru completes the statement that one's mouth becomes defiled. The Portuguese translates someone holding blood in the mouth and spitting; its object follows below.

runs.text: no outro, elle he o q̃ fica primeiro com ſangue cõ

lines.note: The person spitting at another is himself first contaminated with blood. Both abbreviation tildes are retained, including the unhyphenated line-final cõ before taminado.

runs.text: taminado. Acommodaſe ao que murmura de

lines.note: Completes contaminado and explains the proverb's figurative application to someone who speaks ill of others. The Portuguese verb is murmura, not a Japanese example.
Others completes the explanation of slander: the slanderer stains himself first. The short final word remains on its own physical row.
Kegare is the noun for dirtiness or impurity, distinct from the preceding inflected verb. The paired Portuguese nouns directly explain this nominal sense.

runs.text: Gallo, ou galinha que tem penas

lines.note: Qegarifa names a cock or hen with feathered feet. The Portuguese capital has the cross-stroke of Gallo, not OCR Callo; the Japanese spelling is retained as printed.
The feathers extend along the feet as far as the claws. Pees and vnhas retain the source's spelling, and the accent in atè is not modernized.
Kegashi, kegasu, kegaita gives the transitive verb for soiling. The historical -aita principal form is retained; it introduces the verse on the following two rows.
The verse recalls washing in the clear current of the Miwa River. Susugiteshi expresses the past washing; the following row supplies the garment's sleeves and a vow not to soil them again.

The speaker will not again soil the sleeves of the robe. The small mark over the o of ſǒdeuo is retained as supplied and visible, despite the ordinary lexical reading sode; it is not silently regularized.

runs.text: Lib. 1. Tendo lauado as mãgas de meus

lines.note: Fox. identifies the quoted source, followed by book 1. The Portuguese translates the washing of the speaker's sleeves; mãgas retains its abbreviation tilde.

runs.text: veſtidos neſte rio não as tornarei mais a ſujar.

lines.note: The translation promises not to soil those garments again after washing them in this river. This completes the literal interpretation of the preceding verse.

runs.text: Entẽdeſe cõ as couſas do mũdo q̃ tinha deixado.

lines.note: The editor explains that the verse concerns worldly things the speaker had abandoned. The four printed abbreviation tildes remain unexpanded in the canonical text.
Na wo kegasu means staining one's name or reputation. The Portuguese phrase Por nodoa means placing a stain; no modern accent is supplied to the infinitive.

After completing the name-and-reputation gloss, Facuma wo kegasu introduces a written-register expression for defiling paper. Its explanation continues on the next two rows. Second-pass enlargement confirms the separate upright S. label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Sujar o papel com ſua ruim letra. He modo de

lines.note: The expression depreciates one's own handwriting as soiling the paper. The Portuguese explicitly presents it as a manner of speaking, continued below.
Completes the explanation: this is a humble formula used in letters, rather than a literal statement that paper has become dirty.
Kego is explained by tawabure kataru, speaking playfully rather than seriously. The headword begins with Q, not OCR D; pro continues below without a printed hyphen.

runs.text: poſito mas como dezombaria, ou por paßa-

lines.note: Completes proposito and contrasts serious intention with joking or passing the time. Dezombaria retains the printed joined spelling, and paßa- continues into tempo.
After completing passatempo, the paired terms kego and keron denote conversation or disputation of this joking kind. The Portuguese definition continues below.

Completes the description of playful conversation or argument. The final S is the written-register label, not part of the Japanese synonym. Second-pass enlargement confirms the separate upright S. label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
The verb denotes going ahead to inspect or reconnoitre. No- begins notar, and the extended explanation specifies both military scouts and a thief's preliminary inspection.

runs.text: tar, ou eſpiar como ſoldados que vão diante

lines.note: Completes notar and compares the action with soldiers scouting in advance. The relative clause remains connected to the following account of surveying terrain.

runs.text: a descubrir o campo, ou ver a feição da forta-

lines.note: The scouts examine the field or the configuration of a fortress. Descubrir preserves the source's vowel; forta- continues as fortaleza on the next row.

runs.text: leza, &c. ou como o ladrão que nota primeiro

lines.note: Completes fortaleza and adds the comparison with a thief examining premises beforehand. A visible separation after &c. is retained rather than joining it to ou.

runs.text: os cantos da caſa, & o fato que ha, &c.

lines.note: The thief notes the corners of the house and the goods present. Fato here belongs to the list of property being inspected, completing the reconnaissance explanation.

runs.text: Eſpia que vai ver, & notar eſtas

lines.note: The noun denotes the scout or spy who performs the inspection just described. It is a separate entry following the related verb.
Things completes the scout's definition by referring back to the terrain, fortress, house, and goods described above.

runs.text: Hum dos liuros que compos Xaca.

lines.note: Kegon names a Buddhist book, which the gloss attributes to Xaca. That attribution is part of the historical dictionary's wording; Xaca is a Japanese name embedded in Portuguese.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Hũa ſeita das oito que ha em Ia-

lines.note: The second sense identifies Kegon as one of eight sects said to exist in Japan. Ia- continues as the Portuguese place-name Iapão below.
Completes Iapão and gives Kegonjū for members of the sect. The final vowel has a caron, and the Japanese term is an example label rather than embedded Portuguese prose.
This second Qegon entry refers back to Qego, joking speech, not the Buddhist sect. Sore begins the example whose remainder crosses the column boundary.
The maxim says that a gentleman does not speak frivolously. The Portuguese starts 'the wise and' and is completed by 'prudent' at the top of column 2.
Completes the translation carried from column 1: the wise and prudent man does not utter jokes or frivolous remarks.

runs.text: O eſtarem as armas velhas com o

lines.note: Kegire describes old armour whose lacing has deteriorated. The Portuguese armas is explained more precisely by the following reference to the woven thread.

runs.text: fio da tecedura gaſtado, & cortado. Vt,

lines.note: The lacing is worn and severed. Qe- begins the Japanese example kegire shita yoroi; the scan shows a hyphen, not the OCR's italic period.
Kegire shita yoroi means armour with worn-out lacing. Gas- begins the Portuguese gastadas, preserving the visible short s at the line end.
Completes gastadas desta maneira, worn in the particular way just described. The short continuation belongs to the armour example.
The dictionary explains kegime through a feigned thing or dissimulation. Enlargement establishes the ß ligature and cedilla in dißimulação, replacing the garbled OCR ditimulacão.
Kegime ga miyeta describes the underlying truth becoming apparent. The printed paragraph mark before the example was omitted by OCR and is restored; des continues below without a hyphen.

runs.text: cobrioſe a verdade da couſa paleada.

lines.note: Completes descobriose: the truth of the disguised or glossed-over matter was revealed. Paleada is retained as printed, rather than replaced with a modern synonym.
Kei means a view or prospect. Tokoro no kei ga yoi says the place has a good view; its Portuguese translation begins with the final article A.
Completes the example as 'the view of the place is good.' The clause is the translation of the preceding Japanese, not a separate sense.
A different kei means punishment or the execution of justice. The maxim begins kei no utagawashiki, a doubtful matter concerning punishment, and continues below.
The maxim says to weigh doubtful punishment carefully, then contrasts a doubtful claim of merit or service. The printed circumflex in côno is retained.
Caronjeyo completes the contrasting instruction about doubtful merit. The Portuguese introduces the conditions under which the maxim applies rather than translating each word mechanically.

runs.text: duuida ſobre caſtigar, ou matar alguem, exa-

lines.note: When there is doubt about punishing or killing someone, examination is required. Exa- begins examina, which is completed on the next physical row.

runs.text: mina, & pondera bem: quando ouuer duuida

lines.note: Completes the command to examine and weigh matters carefully, then introduces doubt about a service. The scan has duuida, including the u omitted by OCR.

runs.text: ſe he ſeruiço dalgũ vaſalo não faças tanto ca-

lines.note: The second case concerns whether a vassal has rendered service: the reader is told not to scrutinize it so heavily. Ca- continues into caso below.

runs.text: ſo ainda que logo o julgues por ſeruiço.

lines.note: Completes caso and allows the deed to be accepted promptly as service. This closes the contrast between caution in punishment and generosity in recognizing merit.

runs.text: Muitos caualos juntos de dous em do-

lines.note: Keiba is described as horses brought together in pairs for racing. Dous is divided across the physical line ending and must not be joined in the transcription.

runs.text: us pera correr à profia como ſe faz no Miaco

lines.note: Completes dous and explains racing in competition, as practised in Miaco. Miaco is a Japanese place-name occurring inside the Portuguese explanation.
The races take place at a particular time. Kamo no keiba wo begins the example about observing the races at Kamo, completed by miru below.

runs.text: Ver eſta junta de caualos pera correr

lines.note: Miru completes the example, seeing the assembly of horses for racing. The Portuguese translation specifies the location on the following row.

runs.text: da poſta na quelle lugar Camo.

lines.note: Completes the description of horse-racing at Camo. The printed na quelle separation is retained, and Camo is a Japanese name within Portuguese prose.
Keibat denotes execution by judicial authority. The bare final t is retained in both headword and example; the example's verb follows below.
Suru completes keibat suru, carrying out a judicial execution. This short Japanese continuation is a body row, not a catchword.

runs.text: Vara, ou rota com que açoutão na

lines.note: Keiben is a rod or cane used for judicial whipping. The Portuguese location is completed by China on the next physical row.
Completes the definition as an instrument of judicial punishment in China. This is part of the dictionary's description, not an additional headword.
Keibi denotes something slight or of small quantity. The following adjectival and adverbial forms belong to this same semantic group.
Keibina is the adjectival form, with Idem referring to the preceding smallness sense. The initial Q is upright roman type, not the OCR's italic O.
Keibini is marked as an adverb; the example concedes that something is slight. The Portuguese begins Posto, with visible s rather than the OCR's r in the line-final fragment.
Completes Posto que seja pouquidade, 'although it be a small amount.' It explains the concessive gozaredomo rather than giving a new entry.
Keibo is equated with Mamafaua and glossed as stepmother. The initial Q is restored to roman type; the unusual internal spelling of the Japanese synonym is preserved.

runs.text: Deſejo importuno com que hum por

lines.note: Keibō denotes an importunate desire to obtain something. The caron distinguishes its printed form from the preceding unaccented keibo, stepmother.

runs.text: todas as vias quer auer algũa couſa, ou toma-

lines.note: The desire pursues possession by every means, even taking the object. Auer is the historical spelling, and toma- is physically divided before the following pronoun.
Completes taking the thing by force, then gives keibō suru. The visible separation De ſejar is retained rather than silently joining the Portuguese infinitive.
Completes the example's gloss as desiring in the manner just described, namely insistently and potentially by force.

runs.text: Fruita, ou comer que ha em certo,

lines.note: Keibut refers to seasonal fruit or food. The printed final t and historical Fruita remain unchanged; the seasonal restriction is developed below.

runs.text: & determinado tempo do anno como peras, &

lines.note: The food belongs to a fixed time of year, with pears as the first example. This continues the seasonal definition rather than introducing an unrelated list.
Grapes in September complete the examples. Toki no keibut begins the phrase about assembling seasonal delicacies for hospitality, split after qei-.
The Japanese phrase means entertaining guests with a selection of seasonal foods. The final t before uo is preserved rather than expanded to a modern open syllable.

runs.text: todas as fruitas, & iguarias de todos os tem-

lines.note: The Portuguese describes gathering fruits and delicacies from the various seasons. Tem- continues as tempos; no text is missing at the column edge.
Completes tempos do anno and the act of welcoming and entertaining guests. The seasonal-food example ends here.

Keichō is equated with niwatori and glossed as a cock or hen. The circumflex and the written-register label are preserved. Second-pass enlargement confirms the separate upright S. label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Exercicio, ou enſayo de couſas que hum

lines.note: Keiko means practice or rehearsal of things already learned. The relative clause continues below and makes the acquired-skill sense explicit.
Completes the practice definition and gives keiko suru, to practise. The Japanese example remains roman, distinct from the italic Portuguese introduction.
Keikoku is explained by kuni katamuku, a kingdom falling into ruin. The Portuguese verb is divided after deſ- at the physical line ending.

Completes destruindo and marks the expression as written usage. This short row belongs to the political sense, not the following homograph. Second-pass enlargement confirms the separate upright S. label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

A separate keikoku means valleys, explained by the repeated tani. The lower-right Qeidacu is a catchword for the next page and is not part of this body row. Second-pass enlargement confirms the separate upright S. label and two distinct l letters in Valles, correcting OCR Vales. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Anticipates Qeidacu. at the opening of f379; this lower-right item is catchword furniture, not another body line.
